title: Semantic-Assisted Joint Channel Estimation and Symbol Detection for MU-MIMO Systems
authors: Hao Chang; Chentao Yue; Haiyao Yu; Yonghui Li; Branka Vucetic; Wibowo Hardjawana
abstract: This paper presents a semantic-assisted joint channel estimation and symbol detection (Sem-JCED) receiver framework for text transmission in multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) systems. Sem-JCED integrates a linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) channel estimator, an expectation propagation (EP) symbol detector, and a semantic corrector based on ByT5, a byte-level language model. At each outer iteration, LMMSE estimates the channel from known pilots and data symbol feedback, and EP detects the data symbols. ByT5 then maps the data symbol probabilities to byte probabilities, which provide soft symbol statistics and semantic priors for feedback to LMMSE and EP, respectively, in the next iteration. Simulation results show that Sem-JCED requires about 7~dB lower signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) than conventional JCED to reach a bit error rate (BER) of $1\times10^{-2}$ with four users and four receive antennas, and outperforms maximum-likelihood detection with perfect channel knowledge over the simulated SNR range.

title: Semantic Anchor Communication System for Point Cloud Transmission in Internet of Vehicles
authors: Ruixing Ren; Junhui Zhao; Wei Zhao; Gaoxin Zhang; Xiaoming Wang
abstract: Joint transmission of point cloud geometry and semantics under bandwidth constraints is required for cooperative perception in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). Per-point semantics cannot be explicitly preserved by existing geometric compression methods, while interpretable three-dimensional point sets cannot be directly reconstructed via task-feature communication. The paper proposes a spatial semantic anchor communication system. Distinct from global codewords and task features, anchors with explicit coordinates are employed as transmission units. Local shape descriptors and category labels are bound to a unified spatial reference, preserving the correspondence between local position, shape and semantics. At the transmitter, anchor representations are extracted and then converted into digital frames through fixed-point quantization and lossless compression.Atthereceiver,labeledpoint clouds are reconstructed through anchor-constrained local expansion, and pose-aligned multi-view observations are fused. On the 500-frame SemanticPOSS test set, the results demonstrate that spatial semantic anchors enable interpretable joint reconstruction and fusion of geometry and semantics with low transmission overhead.
arxiv_comment: 10 pages, 3 figures

title: Federated Learning for Semantic Communications over Multiple Access Channels
authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu; Tugba Erpek; Yi Shi
abstract: This paper presents a federated learning (FL) framework for semantic communication (SemCom) over the multiple access channel (MAC), where multiple distributed transmitters simultaneously convey semantic information to a common receiver using end-to-end learned semantic representations. Semantic feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission, and semantic inference are jointly optimized through FL-based SemCom. Unlike conventional SemCom systems that train users independently, simultaneous semantic transmissions over the MAC enable concurrent training of multiple transmitters within the same transmission interval, thereby reducing training overhead and channel usage. Federated semantic aggregation is incorporated with shared and personalized encoder components, allowing transmitters with limited local training data to benefit from semantic representations learned from transmitters possessing larger datasets while preserving local adaptation. Evaluated using the CIFAR-10 dataset over fading channels, the proposed approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared wireless access and significantly improves performance under severe data imbalance. In the meantime, simultaneous semantic transmissions can significantly reduce training overhead while preserving robust semantic performance across distributed transmitters with heterogeneous local datasets. These results highlight the potential of combining FL and SemCom to support scalable and communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.

title: NLP-based Message Prioritisation for Opportunistic Routing: A Case Study of Nepal Earthquake Emergency Communication
authors: Yihang Cao; Milena Radenkovic
abstract: This dissertation investigates whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) based semantic message prioritisation can improve the treatment of urgent disaster messages in opportunistic emergency communication, using the 2015 Nepal earthquake as a case study. TF IDF with Logistic Regression and BERT are used to classify social media messages into nine humanitarian categories, which are mapped to four routing priorities from P1 to P4. These priorities are integrated into the ONE simulator within a controlled Kathmandu earthquake scenario using a modified Binary Spray and Wait router. BERT achieves higher priority accuracy and P1 recall than Logistic Regression, while reducing under prioritisation and severe priority errors. However, improved NLP performance does not produce uniform network gains. P1 delivery probability remains high and similar across routing conditions, and no consistent latency reduction is observed. The clearest difference appears under buffer pressure, where the BERT condition shows fewer observed ground truth P1 buffer losses than Logistic Regression. The results indicate that semantic prioritisation is most valuable when limited transmission and storage resources are contested, although it cannot overcome mobility and contact constraints in opportunistic networks.

title: TP-JSCC: Efficient Token Pruning and Joint Source-Channel Coding for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration
authors: Zhengxin Li; Chongzhen Tian; Hui Yuan; Hao Liu; Sam Kwong
abstract: Deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) on resource-constrained embodied agents for 3D visual question answering necessitates cloud-edge collaboration. However, offloading massive visual data to the cloud over bandwidth-limited and noisy channels introduces severe latency and transmission distortion. To address this, we propose TP-JSCC, an efficient token pruning and joint source-channel coding method for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration. First, we develop a Local and Global Semantics-based Hybrid Token Pruning (LGS-HTP) module to significantly reduce the visual token count. By decoupling foreground-background tokens and jointly selecting local and global semantics, LGS-HTP effectively reduces redundancy while preserving reasoning-critical tokens. Second, we introduce a lightweight Token Joint Source-Channel Coding (T-JSCC) module to further compress the pruned tokens and ensure their robust transmission over error-prone channels. By employing lightweight cascaded linear layers and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-adaptive mechanism, this module adapts to fluctuating channel conditions while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanQA and SQA3D datasets indicate the exceptional efficiency and robustness of our approach. Specifically, on ScanQA validation set, the LGS-HTP module could achieve 90% pruning ratio while incurring less than a 1% CIDEr loss. Building on this, the T-JSCC further compresses the tokens by 18 times, resulting in an overall 180 times data volume reduction for robust transmission, while saving 90% in computational complexity for LVLM deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhui0325/TP-JSCC.

title: Dynamic Feature-Embedding Communication via Codebook Distillation for Federated Recommendation
authors: Mingzhe Han; Jiahao Liu; Dongsheng Li; Jiankui Zhou; Yaqiong Li; Ning Gu; Peng Zhang; Tun Lu
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: Federated recommendation systems commonly protect user privacy by keeping user parameters on local devices, while exchanging item parameters for collaborative model training. However, such item parameters usually model items independently and suffer from both efficiency and effectiveness challenges, making communication costs grow with the item space and limiting cross-item generalization and robustness to noisy feedback. To address these limitations, we propose to model items via shared latent feature embeddings for communication. Residual Quantization (RQ) provides a natural way to instantiate this communication by representing each item with a short sequence of discrete code IDs, i.e., Semantic IDs (SIDs). However, directly applying centralized and static RQ-based recommendation to federated learning is non-trivial due to 1) private and biased historical interactions and 2) evolving collaborative information. We propose RQFedRec, an RQ-based federated recommendation framework for dynamic feature-embedding communication. To construct globally aligned codebooks without accessing private interactions, RQFedRec introduces an information distillation module. Each client first learns item embeddings that encode local collaborative information from private interactions, and then distills such information into feature-indexed codebooks under globally shared SIDs, making sparse and biased local signals more compatible with server aggregation. To adapt to evolving collaborative information, RQFedRec introduces a self-refining SID update module that dynamically refines global SID assignments from aggregated codebooks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RQFedRec improves recommendation performance and reduces communication costs without relying on semantic information, while further benefiting from public semantics when available. Code is available at https://github.com/Mingzhe-Han/RQFedRec.

title: Owning the narrative: Exploring the impact of a creative storytelling intervention on stigma and empowerment among persons affected by leprosy in Pakistan
authors: Nervana Ibrahim; Anil Fastenau; Abdul Salam; Fabian Schlumberger; Matthew Dean Willis; Lucy Mckane; Ali Murtaza; Maaike Leonie Seekles; Laura Dean; India Hotopf
abstract: Abstract Introduction Despite being curable, leprosy-related stigma in Pakistan persists, undermining dignity, delaying care, and hindering progress toward zero-leprosy targets. Empowerment is critical in counteracting stigma and restoring agency among affected persons. Participatory, contact-based storytelling has potential to reduce stigma and strengthen empowerment, but evidence remains limited. This study evaluates a participatory storytelling intervention involving persons affected by leprosy in Karachi. Objectives This study investigates how a participatory storytelling intervention influences stigma and empowerment among persons affected by leprosy in Pakistan. It explores changes in participants’ experiences, examines the mechanisms through which storytelling engages with stigma and identifies practical insights to strengthen future intervention design. Methods We conducted a qualitative study following the 2024–25 participatory storytelling pilot at MALC, Karachi. Persons affected by leprosy who participated in the intervention were purposively sampled (age 30-65 years); sixteen participated in photovoice and fourteen completed in-depth interviews (IDIs) (thirteen of which had also participated in photovoice) (total n= 17). Data were analysed thematically using the Social Ecological Model (SEM). Results The programme supported a shift from shame and concealment to greater self-acceptance, confidence and openness. Peer groups and creative storytelling built solidarity, a sense of belonging and transferable skills, while organisational endorsement enhanced participants’ visibility and roles. However, stigma remained reinforced by community misconceptions, gender norms and practical barriers. Overall, the intervention’s greatest effect was at the individual level, reducing self and anticipated stigma, with intrapersonal empowerment emerging as the primary gain. Conclusion Participatory storytelling enhanced identity and empowerment, but broader social change remained constrained by gender norms, visible disability, and structural barriers. Strengthening impact requires sustained community contact, supported peer educators, inclusive outreach to women and persons with visible impairments, and links to socioeconomic opportunities. Embedding peer-led storytelling within skin NTD services and national and WHO strategies can support community ownership and sustainability. Author summary Leprosy is a curable disease, yet many people affected by it continue to experience stigma that affects their mental health, confidence, relationships and health seeking behaviour. In Pakistan, stigma remains a major barrier to achieving zero-leprosy goals and improving quality of life. Our study explored the degree to which a participatory storytelling intervention, where persons affected by leprosy share their experiences through creative methods, supported empowerment and reduced stigma. We conducted a qualitative study with participants involved in a storytelling pilot intervention in Karachi, using interviews and photovoice to explore their experiences. Participants described the transition from shame and secrecy toward openness, greater self-confidence and self-acceptance. The storytelling process encouraged peer support, strengthened social connections and helped participants develop new skills and a stronger sense of identity. However, persistent community misconceptions, gender norms, visible disability and economic constraints limited broader social change. Our findings suggest that participatory storytelling interventions present a promising approach for reducing internalised stigma and strengthening individual empowerment among persons affected by leprosy. To achieve wider impact, storytelling initiatives should be combined with sustained community engagement, inclusive outreach and integration into skin neglected tropical disease (NTD) services and broader social support programmes.

title: Network analysis of teaching self-efficacy and tacit knowledge sharing among clinical nursing preceptors: a multicenter cross-sectional study
authors: Jie Li; Zhining Liu; Chengwei Xu; Ming Jin; Zhiqiang Wang
abstract: Abstract Background: Clinical nursing preceptors play a central role in translating classroom knowledge into clinical competence. Teaching self-efficacy and tacit knowledge sharing are important components of precepting capacity, yet their item-level associations remain unclear. This study examined the network structure of teaching self-efficacy and tacit knowledge sharing among clinical nursing preceptors and identified central and bridge items to inform future preceptor training. Methods: A multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted from February to June 2026 among 1221 clinical nursing preceptors from four hospitals in Guangyuan, Sichuan Province, China. Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire, the Clinical Teacher Tacit Knowledge Sharing Scale, and the Chinese version of the Clinical Nursing Teachers’ Teaching Self-Efficacy Scale. A regularized partial-correlation network was estimated using a Gaussian graphical model with graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. Strength, closeness, betweenness, and bridge strength were calculated. Bootstrapping was used to assess edge accuracy and centrality stability. Network comparison tests were conducted by age, precepting experience, and frequency of preceptor training. Results: The mean teaching self-efficacy score was 167.78 ± 38.44, and the mean tacit knowledge-sharing score was 36.96 ± 4.65. The network included 32 nodes and 234 non-zero edges. The strongest edge connected exchanging work-related experience with nurses and sharing information on key procedural techniques. High strength centrality was observed for items related to creating learning opportunities, multidisciplinary collaboration, and optimizing clinical teaching based on interns’ assessment results. Bridge strength was highest for items related to expressing experience during learning activities, communication guidance, and sharing work-related know-how. The correlation stability coefficient for strength centrality was 0.60. Network structures differed by age group and frequency of preceptor training, but not by precepting experience. Conclusions: Teaching self-efficacy and tacit knowledge sharing among clinical nursing preceptors formed an interconnected item-level network. Learning opportunity creation, feedback-informed teaching adjustment, multidisciplinary collaboration, and tacit knowledge externalization may represent candidate priorities for future preceptor training. Given the cross-sectional self-report design, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory associations rather than causal evidence.

title: A Comparative Conceptual Analysis of "bənê hā'ĕlōhîm" ("Sons of God") in the Qur'ān and Jewish Texts: Examining the Attribution of Polytheism to Jews in the Story of 'Uzayr in Qur'ān
authors: Hamed Reza Karimi Malayer
venue: Journal of World Religions and Interfaith Harmony
abstract: This paper offers a comparative conceptual analysis of the expression bənê hā’ĕlōhîm (בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים, “Sons of God”) within Jewish theology and the Qur’ānic reference to ʿUzayr in verse Q 9:30. Employing an intertextual framework informed by Julia Kristeva’s theory of textual transposition and late antique Qur’anic hermeneutics, this study reassesses the dialogue between the Qur’anic corpus and its Biblical/post-Biblical subtexts. Contrary to conventional exegetical readings that attribute literal polytheism (Shirk) to Jews for this expression, I argue that both traditions fundamentally employ such idioms metaphorically and honorifically, designating spiritual proximity rather than ontological divinity. By analyzing the semantic trajectory along both historical and intertextual axes—particularly through key Qur’ānic terms such as arbāb (“lords”) and dūn Allāh (“apart from God”)—this study challenges traditional polemical readings and repositions the Qur’ān’s theological critique within its broader Late Antique context. Ultimately, this approach facilitates a more nuanced intertextual understanding of monotheism across Abrahamic traditions and contributes to current debates on scriptural semantics and interfaith hermeneutics.

title: A A Comparative Study of Multimodal Discourse in Micro-Learning Videos via Intersemiotic Complementarity Theory
authors: Binyan Ma; Hanxu Liu
venue: English Language Teaching and Linguistics Studies
abstract: With the increasing popularity of online educational videos, how to teach and disseminate these videos has become a challenge for many creators. But few of the current studies discussed the intersemiotic complementarity of micro-learning videos and how to promote their effectiveness through this angle. Based on the intersemiotic complementarity theory, this research explores how the collaborative interaction between micro-learning videos’ image and text affects the effectiveness of teaching and dissemination. This study compares and analyzes the image-text relationship of the two videos, Crash Course (CC) and Home Revise (HR) from ideational, interpersonal and compositional intersemiotic complementarity (IC). The study finds that: (1) For ideational IC, both videos use synonymy, collocation and hyponymy, and repetition is often combined with other relationship types to form a composite type. (2) For interpersonal IC, CC uses a lot of demand shots, and the text mood is diverse, so as to build a sense of interaction. (3) For compositional IC, the layout of CC is more flexible. In contrast, the layout of HR is relatively fixed and monotonous. The results of this study show that good ideational IC can reduce the cognitive burden and promote the teaching effectiveness; highly interactive interpersonal IC can improve audience participation; good compositional IC can balance teaching and fun. This study expands the application of intersemiotic complementarity in video analysis, and also provides inspirations for the design and evaluation of micro-learning videos.

title: Human-AI Communication Symbiosis: How Educators Reconstruct Authority and Identity in the Algorithmic Era
authors: Frederik Masri Gasa; Herma Retno Prabayanti; Novita Damayanti; Imam Sofyan; Tatag Handaka; Dinara Maya Julijanti; Sriyono
venue: International Journal of Technology in Education and Science
abstract: The present schooling system is currently facing a dual disruptive crisis, spurred by the encroachment of social media algorithms and generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). While these forces impact the way students learn and think about information, they also induce an epistemological overhaul in the ecology of instructional communication. Students, with their visual rhetorical frameworks from digital platforms and the use of AI for analytical processing, present an apparent disciplinary crisis for their educators-a communication crisis in disguise. Applying Karl Weick's Sensemaking theory, this paper examines school leaders and Guidance Counselors in Samarinda, Indonesia's understanding of these ambiguities and reconceptualization of their roles. Through qualitative case studies based on teachers' pedagogical narratives, this study shows that teachers' epistemological authority is diminishing as they negotiate the hegemonic algorithmic communication. They respond to the students' fear of cognitive degradation by reorienting from a "knowledge transmitting" communicative practice towards "ethical verifiers" and "empathetic listeners." A Human-AI symbiosis is being created with the machine as information provider and humans as ethical validators and empathic listener. Implications were made for the development of policies related to algorithmic communication literacy and the application of tactical empathy in the classroom.

title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
authors: Andrew Gao; William Gao
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.

title: Going Deeper With Memories
authors: Afshin Khadangi
abstract: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.

title: ProAlign: Progressive Positional and Prototype-Guided Alignment for Aerial-Ground Person Re-Identification
authors: Qiao Li; Jing Chen; Cong Wu; Kun He; Ruiying Du; Lei Tan
abstract: Aerial-Ground Person Re-Identification (AG-ReID) aims to match pedestrian images captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground-based surveillance cameras. The task remains highly challenging due to severe viewpoint discrepancies, frequent occlusions, and substantial domain gaps between aerial and ground imagery. Beyond these observable factors, existing methods often overlook two fundamental structural issues: cumulative positional drift during hierarchical feature extraction and semantic inconsistency across cross-view feature distributions. To address these challenges, we propose ProAlign, a Progressive Positional and Prototype-Guided Alignment Network for AG-ReID. ProAlign comprises two key components: a Layer-wise Progressive Positional Embedding (LPPE) module and a View-Aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (PCL) module. LPPE performs adaptive positional calibration throughout transformer layers by employing conditional positional encoding in shallow layers to mitigate local spatial distortions, while introducing learnable static positional embeddings in deeper layers to reinforce global semantic priors. Meanwhile, PCL maintains view-specific aerial and ground prototypes for each identity and enforces cross-view semantic consistency via a dual-prototype contrastive objective. Extensive experiments on CARGO and two real-world AG-ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ProAlign, achieving state-of-the-art overall retrieval performance on CARGO with improvements of 1.60% in Rank-1 accuracy and 5.01% in mAP over the strongest competing methods.

title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
authors: Kling Team; Dong Chen; Jialu Chen; Xinlong Chen; Yifan Dai; Haotian Dong; Binzong Geng; Yushuo Guan; Minghui Guo; Guanlin He; Guanxiao He; Jingyun Hua; Yanwei Huang; Yiyan Ji; Xueping Jia; Yizhuo Jia; Bozhou Li; Jiaze Li; Min Li; Shihao Li; Shujie Li; Shengyi Liao; Weihong Lin; Shiyuan Liu; Xinyu Liu; Siyang Mao; Xiaoru Qu; Dianmo Sheng; Yang Shi; Jiafu Tang; Longxiang Tang; Yuqi Tang; Chengzhuo Tong; Kuo Wang; Qixun Wang; Rui Wang; Tianduo Wang; Yuran Wang; Zekun Wang; Zihao Wang; Boyang Xia; Yifan Xu; Liu Yang; Zhenlong Yuan; Bohan Zeng; Mujin Zhang; Yuanxing Zhang; Zhicheng Zhang; Zhuoran Zhang; Yuanhong Zheng; Kun Gai; Chengru Song; Pengfei Wan
abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

title: Learning to Rank Explanations for Recommendation with Language Models
authors: Ben Kabongo; Vincent Guigue
abstract: Recommender systems are ubiquitous on the Web, making understandable explanations essential for users. Although large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate natural-language justifications, evaluating their factual grounding and personalized relevance remains challenging. Statement-level ranking offers an alternative by selecting concise, review-derived explanations, enabling fine-grained and reproducible evaluation using established ranking metrics. However, existing statement ranking methods largely rely on collaborative representations, while semantic enhancements often fail to outperform simple user-history popularity baselines. Moreover, directly adapting language models for personalized statement ranking remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce LMStaR (Language Models for Statement Ranking), a fully text-based framework that formulates personalized explanation ranking as dense retrieval. A query encoder represents the user's interaction history and target-item metadata, while a statement encoder maps candidate explanations into a shared embedding space. Both encoders are jointly adapted through multi-positive contrastive learning to learn personalized relevance. Experiments on Amazon Beauty, Amazon Toys, and Yelp show that LMStaR achieves the highest NDCG@1 across all three domains, outperforming CLER by 1.06--8.25 points (+11.8--65.9%). It also leads top-five ranking on both Amazon datasets, although CLER remains stronger on Yelp. Task-specific adaptation improves all five evaluated backbones and transfers across domains without target-domain fine-tuning. Counterfactual analyses further reveal the importance of user-specific histories. These findings highlight the potential of task-adapted language models for personalized explanation ranking.

title: TAPES: Task-Aligned Joint Predictive Pretraining for Transaction Event Sequences
authors: Ruobing Zuo; Weiyu Han; Huilin He; Haoyu Jiang; Ze Zhao; Jie Sheng; Xiao Tan; Shuai Chen; Tianyi Zhang
abstract: Transaction event sequences support diverse prediction tasks in online commerce and digital financial services. The same transaction records can yield prediction targets with different semantics, including values, changes, and relations to past events. These targets impose different constraints on history representations, but their predictability alone does not establish the downstream utility of a target set. Moreover, target-wise prediction losses do not explicitly model conditional co-occurrence among targets. To address these challenges, we propose TAPES, a task-aligned joint predictive pretraining framework for transaction sequences. TAPES constructs a finite collection of candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations. It selects a target set according to the downstream utility of representations learned through short joint pretraining trials under matched budgets. It then reinitializes the encoder and pretrains it on the selected targets through a joint likelihood parameterized by a shared discrete latent variable, before downstream supervised adaptation. Experiments in a real-world transaction-risk setting and on multiple public financial benchmarks spanning diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that TAPES outperforms representative baselines. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of predictive target selection and joint modeling.

title: All-For-One: Distilling Visual Foundation Models to a Fast, Memory-Efficient Visuomotor Policy
authors: Byungkun Lee; Minho Park; Hojoon Lee; Dongyoon Hwang; Donghu Kim; Hyunseung Kim; Kyungmin Lee; Yunho Kim; Jaegul Choo
abstract: Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) provide semantic cues such as depth and segmentation useful for robotic manipulation, but directly deploying them in closed-loop control is impractical due to high computational cost, temporal inconsistency, and distribution shift between static internet images and egocentric robot observations. We propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage distillation framework that leverages VFMs strictly as privileged information during training, using downstream robotic data. Following the privileged learning paradigm, AFO decouples semantic representation learning from inference-time policy execution. In the All stage, a teacher policy fuses RGB observations with outputs from multiple VFMs to learn a semantically enriched representation. In the For-One stage, this knowledge is distilled in-distribution into a lightweight RGB-only student policy. Evaluated on two Adroit tasks and five MetaWorld tasks in simulation, as well as three real-world manipulation tasks, AFO outperforms prior foundation-model-based approaches while using over 30x fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50x lower latency than its own teacher in simulation benchmarks, providing an efficient pathway for transferring foundation-model knowledge to robotic control.

title: Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy for Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
authors: Mingcong Li; Yihan Zhou; Jiayu Qu; Xueyang Guo; Yilin Mo
abstract: Diffusion-based policies have achieved strong performance on single-task robotic manipulation. However, a single model trained jointly on multiple tasks consistently underperforms the per-task specialists trained on the same demonstrations. We focus on two challenges. First, the convolutional encoders commonly used in diffusion-based policies produce visual conditions that are not discriminative enough. Second, gradients from incompatible action modes update the shared denoiser's dense parameters along the same directions, causing destructive interference during joint training. To address both, we propose SR-DP (Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy). A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens, a task-discriminative visual condition for tasks that share a workspace. We first train the denoiser as a standard diffusion policy, then decompose selected linear layers by SVD into a frozen basis of orthogonal rank-one experts, adapted through spectral routing and Householder input rotations. On six RoboTwin tasks, SR-DP averages a 68.4% success rate, surpassing multi-task VO-DP by 21.8 points and the strongest per-task baseline by 3.8 points. On four real-world bimanual tasks, Stage 2 reaches a 43.0% average success rate and improves over Stage 1 by 19.0 points.

title: DynOSeg: Dynamic Object Segmentation via Motion-Geometry Fusion
authors: Xu Han; Yiduo Wang; Yiran Wang; Viorela Ila
abstract: Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) detects and separates dynamic objects from the static background in a video, which plays a fundamental role in dynamic-scene understanding. Most MOS methods rely on pure visual motion cues alone, such as optical flow or point tracks, which is inherently ambiguous due to the compounded camera and object motions as well as motion-induced appearance changes, e.g. shadows and reflections. Naive fusion of additional information such as depth and semantics, however, cannot leverage their complementarity to the fullest extent. We therefore propose DynOSeg, a novel MOS approach that takes on a two-stage fusion structure. DynOSeg first combines a geometry-aware residual map and depth encoding into a geometric representation of motion, delineating camera motions and object dynamics. We then further incorporate semantic features to refine object understanding. We have additionally curated a diverse training corpus including CARLA-MOS, a new synthetic urban-driving dataset for MOS training. Our experiments show that DynOSeg consistently outperforms published state-of-the-art MOS methods across a diverse range of datasets. Our code and pretrained models can be found at https://github.com/ACFR-RPG/DynOSeg

title: Do Retrieval Ranking Models Capture Event Order? A Study of Timeline-Constrained Retrieval
authors: Alon Eirew; Lidan Avisar; Kfir Bar; Ido Dagan
abstract: Semantic retrieval models aim to match documents to a query's "meaning", yet it remains unclear whether they successfully encode temporal relations between events in their ranking mechanisms. We investigate this question by studying timeline-constrained document retrieval, where a query is an ordered sequence of natural-language event statements while a relevant document should match those events in a compatible temporal progression. We then test whether widely used dense retrievers and neural rerankers capture such constraints, and whether explicitly preserving temporal order improves ranking, using a controlled setting over a novel focused evaluation collection. Experiments show that state-of-the-art semantic retrievers and rerankers provide only limited improvements over lexical retrieval, suggesting that their semantic matching capabilities do not reliably capture temporal constraints. We then compare a timeline-aware method with both semantic matching and standard rerankers and find that it yields substantial improvements. This demonstrates that considering temporal order can provide a strong ranking signal in this setting, suggesting future research on improving temporal modeling in semantic retrievers.

title: Beyond Faces: Toward Interactive Generative Video Coding via Hybrid Priors
authors: Jianhui Chang; Jialei Zhou; Giuseppe Valenzise; 灏烨 张; Lihu Xiao; Siwei Ma
abstract: Generative face video coding (GFVC) is effective for ultra-lowbitrate talking-head communication, but practical video conferencing often involves hand gestures and face-hand occlusions that are not well handled by existing face-centric pipelines. In such hand-active scenarios, facial and hand motion follow heterogeneous dynamics that complicate compact representation, motion transformation, and reconstruction. To address this, we present a hybrid-prior framework for interactive generative video coding. Our method combines a semantically disentangled structural prior, encoded by compact face-hand landmarks for motion alignment and pose guidance, with a pretrained generative prior, instantiated by a conditional latent diffusion decoder for reconstructing newly emerged or heavily occluded content. Concretely, we introduce a motion-factorized alignment module that decouples facial and hand motion, and a diffusion-based reconstruction stage conditioned on both pose maps and motion-transferred features. We further construct a hand-active benchmark tailored to interactive video conferencing. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves superior reconstruction quality and compression performance over VVC and representative GFVC baselines on both full-frame and hand-region metrics. In particular, it achieves bitrate savings of 60.6% and 76.1% over VVC in terms of LPIPS and DISTS, while also yielding clear improvements in hand-sensitive regions.

title: Large Language Model as Universal Retriever in Industrial-Scale Recommender System
authors: Junguang Jiang; Yanwen Huang; Liu Bin; Xiaoyu Kong; Xinhang Li; Ziru Xu; Han Zhu; Jian Xu; Bo Zheng
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: In real-world recommender systems, different retrieval objectives are typically addressed using task-specific datasets with carefully designed model architectures. We demonstrate that Large Language Models (LLMs) can function as universal retrievers, capable of handling multiple objectives within a generative retrieval framework. To model complex user-item relationships within generative retrieval, we propose multi-query representation. To address the challenge of extremely large candidate sets in industrial recommender systems, we introduce matrix decomposition to boost model learnability, discriminability, and transferability, and we incorporate probabilistic sampling to reduce computation costs. Finally, our Universal Retrieval Model (URM) can adaptively generate a set from tens of millions of candidates based on arbitrary given objective while keeping the latency within tens of milliseconds. Applied to industrial-scale data, URM outperforms expert models elaborately designed for different retrieval objectives on offline experiments and significantly improves the core metric of online advertising platform by $3\%$.

title: Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines
authors: Guanrong Li; Haolin Yang; Xinyu Liu; Zhen Wu; Rui Xia; Xinyu Dai
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: In the era of generative AI, recommender systems are moving from precise prediction to trustworthy generation. Large language models (LLMs) support this shift by inferring user interests and producing natural-language explanations. However, LLM-based recommendation suffers from a fundamental obstacle: popularity bias. Through pre-training on massive corpora, LLMs tend to rely on global statistics and trend signals, yielding recommendations that follow popularity rather than genuine preference. As this bias is entangled in model parameters and is hard to remove directly, we propose Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines (NPRec), a model-agnostic framework that mitigates popularity bias through external semantic intervention. NPRec performs counterfactual refinement to causally separate intrinsic user interests from popularity-driven conformity, producing debiased textual guidelines that reflect actual user preferences. These guidelines are injected at inference time to shift the LLM from unconstrained generation to guided reasoning, without any parameter updates. Serving as explicit premises, they both ground faithful explanations and improve recommendation quality. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that NPRec achieves promising performance in recommendation accuracy, explanation quality, and debiasing capability.

title: Unleashing the Power of LLMs in Dense Retrieval with Query Likelihood Modeling
authors: Hengran Zhang; Keping Bi; Jiafeng Guo; Xiaojie Sun; S. B. Liu; Daiting Shi; Dawei Yin; Xueqi Cheng
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: Dense retrieval is a crucial task in Information Retrieval (IR), serving as the basis for downstream tasks such as re-ranking and augmenting generation. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive semantic understanding capabilities, making them attractive to researchers focusing on dense retrieval. While LLMs, as decoder-style generative models, excel in language generation, they often fall short in modeling global information due to a lack of attention to subsequent tokens. Drawing inspiration from the classical word-based language modeling approach for IR, specifically the query likelihood (QL) model, we aim to leverage the generative strengths of LLMs through QL maximization. Rather than employing QL estimation for document ranking, we propose an auxiliary task of QL maximization to enhance the backbone for subsequent contrastive learning of the retriever. We introduce our model, LLM-QL, which incorporates two key components: Attention Block (AB) and Document Corruption (DC). AB blocks the attention of predictive tokens to the document tokens before the document's ending token, while DC corrupts a document by masking a portion of its tokens during prediction. Evaluations on the in-domain (MS MARCO) and out-of-domain dataset (BEIR) indicate LLM-QL's superiority over other LLM-based retrievers. Furthermore, comprehensive analyses also validate the efficacy of LLM-QL and its components.

title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation
authors: Efthymios Georgiou; Ioannis Kakogeorgiou; Sarah Brüningk
abstract: Transfer learning from natural images is standard in supervised and increasingly adopted in self-supervised medical image analysis, but its role in generative modelling, and in particular diffusion denoisers, remains underexplored. Medical diffusion models typically train the denoiser from scratch, with no systematic evaluation of natural-image transfer. We analyse this across latent and pixel paradigms, model sizes (131M-952M) and two radiology datasets (RadImageNet, BraTS), and ask which aspects of transfer support generation. We find that: i) Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation, by 21-34% relative gFID in pixel space against 14% in latent space, where the tokeniser supplies much of the prior. gFID gains mirror downstream pathology classification and radiomic-feature FD, both proxies for clinical fidelity. ii) Benefits reflect spatial structure, not semantics: semantic probing does not predict generation quality, whereas a spatial-structure metric adapted to internal denoiser representations tracks gFID at $|r|=0.85$, positioning spatial organisation as a channel through which pretraining manifests. iii) Mixed-domain denoiser training shows that natural and medical images share similar layer-wise representations up to the late blocks, and mixing natural images into medical training improves fidelity. iv) Transfer benefit is tied to natural image initialisation, outperforming in-domain medical pretraining and several reinitialisation schemes. Overall, natural image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in our setup. Code is available at https://github.com/CAIROLab-Bern/rad-dit

title: Flat Features, Detailed Images? Simple Detail Control for Diffusion Transformers
authors: Qingtao Yu; Zhen Wang; Jiyang Zheng; Minghao Sun; Hongdong Li; Dylan Campbell
abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly used to encourage text-to-image models to generate more detailed images. However, it does not provide reliable, continuous, or disentangled control. We analyze feature tokens produced with and without detail-enhancing prompts across six diffusion transformers and observe a common pattern: these prompts tend to increase the entropy of each token's energy distribution while largely preserving its ordering. That is, flattening the distribution increases the level of detail. Motivated by this counter-intuitive finding, we introduce a simple training-free approach that continuously adjusts the level of detail according to a scalar. Specifically, it shifts the squared channel magnitudes of each token toward a higher entropy distribution with a time-aware scheduler to concentrate the intervention at intermediate sampling steps. Across extensive experiments on different types of diffusion transformers, we show that our approach provides continuous control over detail metrics while largely preserving image quality and semantic structure. It requires only a few lines of code and adds negligible inference time overhead.

title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
authors: Haoqing Wang; Xiaoyi Zhang; Sicheng Fan; Zhexin Zhang; Xinjie Zhang; Jiahao Li; Bin Li; Yan Lu
abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.

title: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version)
authors: Jens Sprengers; Marton Bognar; Lesly-Ann Daniel; Frank Piessens
abstract: Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a microarchitectural optimization recently introduced in mainstream desktop and server CPUs. Although DMPs offer performance improvements, they have been shown to enable side-channel leakage of secrets, even from constant-time code that has been hardened against Spectre attacks. Unfortunately, existing defenses either incur significant performance overhead or, as we show, fail to prevent all DMP leakage. In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture---without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.

title: Semantic Transferability of Generative Rate-Distortion-Perception Systems
authors: Jinwan Jeon; Seoyeon Hwang; Sung Hoon Lim
abstract: Generative lossy compression combines a rate-limited representation with a stochastic decoder that preserves source-dependent information while generating unresolved detail. We ask what remains reusable when a rate-distortion-perception (RDP) system selected for one operating point is transferred to a prescribed conditional-generation task. We distinguish the single-letter RDP factorization from its block-code implementation and compare Full Redesign with three increasingly restrictive transfer strategies. Renderer-Only Transfer retains only the renderer and redesigns semantic steering. Representation-Induced Transfer additionally retains the semantic latent law induced by the original representation. Full-Model Transfer retains a compatible RDP code, marginalizing over the task conditional law to form its semantic encoder. For finite alphabets, we characterize Renderer-Only Transfer's exact compression-common-randomness rate region, renderer-hull controllability condition, and compression-rate penalty relative to Full Redesign. Under unlimited common randomness, this penalty is the minimum residual semantic information $I(S;U|X)$ forced by the inherited renderer. Representation-Induced Transfer is exact if and only if the semantic condition depends on the source only through the recurrent-class label $C$ of the end-to-end RDP test channel. Every compatible RDP code reused under Full-Model Transfer preserves $C$ and supports every task satisfying $X-C-S$. Any additionally transferable within-class semantic dependence must satisfy $I(S;X|C)\le R_0-H(C)$, where $R_0$ is the inherited compression rate. The bound is exact when $R_0=H(C)$. A scalar Gaussian specialization yields a renderer-noise controllability threshold, a closed-form transfer penalty, and examples of identical Gaussian RDP test channels with different Renderer-Only Transfer capabilities.

title: AlphaCast: A Human Wisdom-LLM Intelligence Co-Reasoning Framework for Time Series Forecasting
authors: Xiaohan Zhang; Tian Gao; Mingyue Cheng; Bokai Pan; Ze Guo; Ying Liu; Xiaoyu Tao; Qi Liu
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: Time series forecasting is typically treated as a single-pass numerical prediction task based on historical observations. However, real-world forecasting often requires expert-like reasoning, where temporal patterns, contextual cues, case-based references, and domain knowledge are jointly considered and iteratively revised. Existing statistical, deep learning, foundation, and LLM-based forecasting models mainly rely on pattern fitting, direct prompting, or static context augmentation, leaving interactive and reflective forecasting insufficiently explored. In this work, we propose AlphaCast, a human wisdom-LLM intelligence co-reasoning framework for interactive time series forecasting. AlphaCast does not require real-time human intervention; instead, it operationalizes human wisdom as structured forecasting support, including time-series features, contextual cues, case-based references, and domain knowledge. Built upon an expert-like think-forecast-reflect workflow, AlphaCast comprises three agents: an Investigator that constructs forecasting context from available evidence, a Generator that produces context-grounded forecasts, and a Reflector that evaluates plausibility and provides feedback for refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AlphaCast improves forecasting accuracy and produces interpretable forecast explanations, offering a promising step toward interactive and context-aware time series forecasting.

title: OneMall: One Architecture, More Scenarios — End-to-End Generative Recommender Family for E-commerce
authors: Kun Zhang; Jingming Zhang; Wei Cheng; Yansong Cheng; Jiaqi Zhang; Jiangxia Cao; Hao Lu; Xu Zhang; Haixiang Gan; Tenglong Wang; Ximing Zhang; Boyang Xia; Kuo Cai; Hongjian Dou; Jinkai Yu; Ming-xing Wen; Qiang Luo; Zhaojie Liu
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: In the wave of generative recommendation, we present OneMall, an end-to-end generative recommendation framework tailored for e-commerce services at Kuaishou. Our OneMall systematically unifies the e-commerce's multiple item distribution scenarios, such as Product-card, short-video and live-streaming. Specifically, it comprises three key components, aligning the entire model training pipeline to the LLM's pre-training/post-training: (1) E-commerce Semantic Tokenizer: we provide a tokenizer solution that captures both real-world semantics and business-specific item relations across different scenarios; (2) Transformer-based Architecture: we largely utilize Transformer as our model backbone, e.g., employing Query-Former for long sequence compression, Cross-Attention for multi-behavior sequence fusion, and Sparse MoE for scalable auto-regressive generation; (3) Reinforcement Learning Pipeline: we further connect retrieval and ranking models via RL, enabling the ranking model to serve as a reward signal for end-to-end policy retrieval model optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneMall achieves consistent improvements across all e-commerce scenarios: +13.01\% GMV in product-card, +15.32\% Orders in Short-Video, and +2.78\% Orders in Live-Streaming. OneMall has been deployed, serving over 400 million daily active users at Kuaishou.

title: Efficient Generative Retrieval for E-commerce Search with Semantic Cluster IDs and Expert-Guided RL
authors: Jianbo Zhu; Xing Fang; Jing Wang; Mingmin Jin; Bokang Wang; Guangxin Song; Zhenyu Xie; Junjie Bai
venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: Generative retrieval offers a promising alternative by unifying the fragmented multi-stage retrieval process into a single end-to-end model. However, its practical adoption in industrial e-commerce search remains challenging, given the massive and dynamic product catalogs, strict latency requirements, and the need to align retrieval with downstream ranking goals. In this work, we propose a retrieval framework tailored for real-world recall scenarios, positioning generative retrieval as a recall-stage supplement rather than an end-to-end replacement. Our method, CQ-SID (Category-and-Query constrained Semantic ID), employs category-aware and query-item contrastive learning along with Residual Quantized VAEs to encode items into hierarchical semantic cluster identifiers, significantly reducing beam search complexity. Additionally, we develop EG-GRPO (Expert-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning approach that aligns generative recall with downstream ranking under sparse rewards by injecting ground-truth samples to stabilize training. Offline experiments on TmallAPP search logs show that CQ-SID achieves up to 26.76% and 11.11% relative gains in semantic and personalized click hitrate over RQ-VAE baselines, while halving beam search size. EG-GRPO further improves multi-objective performance. Online A/B tests confirm gains in GMV (+1.15%) and UCTCVR (+0.40%). The generative recall channel now contributes substantially in production, accounting for over 50.25% of exposures, 58.96% of clicks, and 72.63% of purchases, demonstrating a viable path for deploying generative retrieval in real-world e-commerce systems.
